query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A single-step vapor-phase infiltration of a Cu precursor onto pre‐formed W surfaces will create a conformal, atomic‐scale Cu coating that, upon subsequent sintering, dramatically improves interfacial bonding and minimizes voids and phase separation relative to conventional powder infiltration or sintering techniques.
generation.material_initial_state: Pre-sintered or partially sintered W particles (or connected regions) embedded in or adjacent to a porous Cu matrix that currently exhibits nonuniform interfaces and voids.
generation.intervention: Introduce a vapor-phase infiltration step that deposits a thin, uniform Cu layer on all exposed W surfaces prior to final consolidation/sintering.
generation.conditions: Processing should occur at temperatures below the boiling point of Cu and under controlled low-pressure atmospheres to ensure a gentle deposition and subsequent sintering; service conditions are similar to fusion-reactor joints where high thermal loads and irradiation occur.
generation.structural_mediator: A nearly perfect, void-free Cu–W interface established by the conformal Cu coating, which enhances diffusion bonding during sintering and reduces defects that compromise thermal transport and mechanical strength.
generation.mechanism: The Cu layer deposited in the vapor phase bonds strongly to the tungsten, promoting uniform interfacial contact via atomic-scale diffusion during post-deposition sintering. This leads to a continuous metal–metal bond, thereby preventing phase separation and void formation that otherwise deteriorate thermal and mechanical performance under reactor conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventional methods (e.g., spark-plasma sintering or mechanical alloying of vapor-coated powders), the composite made with the vapor-phase infiltration intervention is expected to exhibit significantly higher thermal conductivity and improved mechanical durability under irradiation.
generation.baseline: Existing fabrication methods such as mechanically alloyed composites or vapor-coated powders sintered without the vapor-phase infiltration step, which suffer from interface voids and phase separation.
generation.boundary: The intervention is applicable under processing temperatures maintained below Cu boiling point and designed for service in high-temperature, irradiative fusion-reactor joint environments.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements in thermal conductivity and mechanical strength, as well as long-term irradiation performance, are uncertain until experimentally validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of W–Cu composite samples: one set using the proposed vapor-phase infiltration technique and one set using the conventional processing route. Process both sets under identical final sintering conditions and then subject them to simulated fusion-reactor irradiation cycles. Evaluate the composites using microstructural imaging and performance testing.
measurements: Interface quality via SEM/TEM (quantifying void fraction and bonding continuity)
Thermal conductivity measurements before and after irradiation
Mechanical strength testing (e.g., tensile or compressive tests) pre- and post-irradiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the vapor-phase infiltrated samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements (e.g., a >20% enhancement in thermal conductivity and mechanical durability) relative to the baseline composites under similar testing conditions, the hypothesis will be falsified.
